Yes. In these results, LLMs can suggest new materials-science experiments without training a task-specific model, by using pretrained knowledge with prompting or few-shot interaction rather than supervised retraining [1, 2, 10]. In particular, an LLM-based active-learning framework proposes experiments directly from text descriptions and, in an iterative few-shot setting, outperformed conventional ML across several materials datasets while reducing the number of experiments needed to find top candidates [1]. LLMs were also used as analogy-driven hypothesis generators to propose novel battery-material candidates beyond established compositional spaces [2].

The papers differ in how “training-free” is used. One focuses on experiment selection in an active-learning loop for materials datasets [1], while another emphasizes analogical reasoning for generating new battery materials [2]. A broader review also says LLMs can coordinate multi-agent experimental systems and laboratory automation in materials discovery workflows, though it does not specifically frame this as training-free experiment suggestion [4].
